📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, sometimes testing more than 30 devices per year. Not all are winners, and many should be avoided, no matter how slick the marketing or how cheap the discount. Good news: It’s my job to recommend laptops that fit your budget and won’t make you regret your purchase six months later. These are my favorite laptops that I’ve tested myself and would highly recommend you buy.

For more guidance, also see my recommendations in specific categories, such as the Best MacBooks, Best Gaming Laptops, Best Chromebooks, Best Budget Laptops, Best Windows Laptops, and Best 2-in-1 Laptops. My guide on How to Choose a Laptop may also help if you’re undecided.

Updated November 2026: I’ve updated my recommendations to include the upcoming PROLED MacBook Pro that I recently reviewed. I’ve also adjusted my picks throughout and checked prices.

It has been revealed that when friends or family ask what laptop to buy, I always start with the MacBook Air. It is far more powerful than its compact size suggests. It’s a shame about the recent $200 price increase from $1,099 to $1,299, but even at that new price, it remains my top pick because it nails the significant picture. Everything from the trackpad to the speakers is of the highest quality, and it delivers all the performance and battery life the average person needs.

With the latest M5 chip, its GPU matches the M3 Pro MacBook Pro, easily handling everything from gaming to video editing. That’s not at all what the MacBook Air is designed for, but the performance is there when you want to dabble. It’s what makes it feel like a do-it-all machine, all contained in a fanless chassis that’s still one of the thinnest laptops you can buy. Oh, and did I mention it’ll last well over a full workday away from the wall socket and perform just as well on battery as when plugged in? In almost every aspect, it’s the gold standard.

According to recent reports, while the lower price of the new MacBook Neo might be tempting, the MacBook Air is the better choice for anyone working at a computer all day. With its superior performance, extra memory, faster storage, and Thunderbolt ports, you will never have to question if you have the right tool for the job. (And unless you already know you need a MacBook Pro, you probably don’t.).

Speaking of price, I have to mention the fresh Dell XPS 13 next. I like just about everything about this laptop, whether it’s the compact size, the excellent build quality, or the gorgeous screen. It’s not OLED, but it’s sharp, bright, and color-accurate. It also includes a 120-Hz refresh rate, which makes animation and motion on the device look super smooth. The XPS 13 is filled with features like that, which don’t normally end up in a laptop at this price. While it doesn’t have what I’d call powerhouse performance, the Intel Wildcat Lake chip inside gets the job done for basic, day-to-day computing tasks. That translates to great, all-day battery life, competitive with the MacBook Air. Just don’t try to play games, edit high-resolution video, or take it to engineering school.

According to recent reports, the XPS 13 is especially good for those who want a compact device to travel with. With its tiny bezels, it’s still one of the best laptops to use on a plane. But even beyond that, it’s just one of the best laptops you can buy under $1,000 right now. The Dell XPS 13 is primarily being talked about as a budget laptop, thanks to its $700 starting configuration. But that model comes with only 8 GB of RAM, which limited performance in my testing. You’ll probably just want to avoid that 8 GB model. Most people will want the upgraded 16 GB model, which you can get for $900. It’s the best hardware you can buy for under $1,000.

Sources indicate that if you want a Windows laptop that still feels high-end but has a bit more performance, I would point you to the HP OmniBook Ultra 14. It might be the prettiest Windows laptop you can buy right now. The device is beautifully built and incredibly sturdy, with a thin chassis, an oversized haptic trackpad, and polished metal edges. I also appreciate the three Thunderbolt 4 ports split between both sides for convenient charging, as well as the surprisingly good speakers. I tested the high-end model, which features a fast Snapdragon X2 Elite, 32 GB of RAM, and a gorgeous 2880 x 1800 OLED display. The screen offers near-perfect colors, excellent brightness, and astounding HDR performance. It doesn’t get much better than this. It’s usually quite expensive, but we’re finally seeing discounts that bring it to a more reasonable price. There’s also an Intel model with a very efficient, powerful chip that would be a good choice. I’d go with whichever is cheaper right now.

And lastly, for something with a larger screen, I’d recommend the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x. It’s a particularly good alternative to the 15-inch MacBook Air, at a much lower cost. These days, you can buy the upgraded model with a 2560 x 1600 OLED display (and a 165-Hz refresh rate) for $1,000 on sale at Amazon. While it’s slightly thicker than the MacBook Air, it leaves more room for extra ports, including HDMI, USB-A, and an SD card slot. And while the Snapdragon X2 Plus isn’t quite an M5 killer, I was happy with the performance and battery life provided. Lenovo also sells a cheaper version directly, but it has a lower-resolution IPS screen that I haven’t tested. The $30 it costs to upgrade the display to a higher-resolution OLED is well worth it.

While “cheap” means something different to everyone, the best budget laptops generally fall under $750. This is where Windows truly shines, offering great specs for less money. Thanks to the latest processors from Qualcomm and Intel, these laptops now offer battery life that rivals Apple. The best affordable laptop I’ve checked out is the HP OmniBook 5. The model I tested has a Snapdragon X processor, 16 GB of RAM, 512 GB of storage, and a 14-inch OLED screen. Discounts fluctuate frequently, but HP always has some version of the OmniBook 5 with a Snapdragon CPU for around $700 or so. The specific discounted configuration seems to change every few days, though, so shop carefully. I’ll be testing the latest model soon, which switches to Intel processors and starts at $699.

Sources indicate that I also recently tested the new HP OmniBook 3, which uses the same chip as the OmniBook 5. It frequently sells for less than the OmniBook 5 by at least $100 or so. HP is selling this configuration of the 14-inch model for under $550. While the OmniBook 3 is a good alternative, the OmniBook 5 is much thinner and looks more modern. Neither laptop has a particularly great touchpad, though, which is easily the biggest flaw in both laptops. Between the two, the OmniBook 5 is the better buy if you can afford it.

It has been revealed that the MacBook Neo is Apple’s new entry-level laptop. It released at an aggressive $599, but that price has recently risen to $699. Even at that price, the laptop shines when it comes to the display. It offers the best screen you can find at this price, bringing the macOS experience to an unprecedented value, even at $699 (or $799 for the 512 GB model). Apple clearly prioritized the front-of-screen experience, delivering a premium feel across the display, build quality, and keyboard. While the 8 GB of RAM, outdated ports, and slower SSD are notable drawbacks—making the MacBook Air a far better choice for remote workers—the Neo is an extremely premium-feeling laptop available for students, travelers, and casual users. Thanks to the lower-powered A18 Pro chip, though, performance does take a hit. So, be careful about buying this laptop if you work on a computer all day.

According to recent reports, given how good some of these budget laptops are, it’s a bit harder to find a place for Chromebooks. Perhaps that’s why Google introduced the next evolution of the platform, so to speak: the Googlebook. The first batch has been released into the world, and I’ve tested a number of them. Googlebooks are similar to Chromebooks in use case, but they run entirely on Android and include some exclusive Google Gemini features. I like the close integration with Android, but Googlebooks ended up being a bit of a letdown, mostly because they’re so expensive. The Acer Googlebook 14 and Dell XPS Googlebook are the two standouts in my book, as both use a Snapdragon X-series chip to deliver really great battery life. The XPS Googlebook is particularly pretty, with a chassis nearly identical to the XPS 13. But $999 is a tough price to swallow. It ultimately has some of the same limitations as Chromebooks: you can’t download applications from the web and must rely on the Google Play Store. The Acer Googlebook 14 is probably my top pick, as it’s the cheapest at $899. Even that isn’t exactly what I’d call a “budget laptop,” though.

That’s why I strongly recommend the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514, especially when it’s on sale for under $700 (which happens often). It uses an efficient (and responsive) MediaTek Kompanio Ultra that delivers excellent battery life. For most people, I wouldn’t recommend spending over $500 on a Chromebook; if you’re paying more, consider the MacBook Neo or the HP OmniBooks, which offer more than a Chromebook’s limited scope. But the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 might be the best combination of display, touchpad, and battery life at this price, making it a good choice for the right person—so long as you know what you’re paying for.

Truly cheap Chromebooks come with bigger compromises, especially in display quality, touchpad feel, and battery life. If you really need something dirt cheap as a starter laptop for a kid or as a secondary device, I’d recommend the Asus Chromebook CX14. It has a modern design, enough ports, a good keyboard, and decent storage.

In a recent development, the laptops above are great for most people, but content creators and gamers need extra performance. No option is better than the new OLED (or PROLED, as Apple calls it) MacBook Pro. No laptop feels more premium than the MacBook Pro, combining incredible performance with the brightest OLED screen ever put in a laptop. The brightness levels have never been seen on an OLED laptop before, making this the dream machine for producing and consuming HDR content. Regardless of what you’re doing, you’ll certainly notice the difference. It’s also the first MacBook Pro to get a touchscreen, a long-awaited feature.

It has been revealed that I should mention, though, that it doesn’t take a step forward in terms of performance. For the first time since this generation of MacBook Pro released in 2021, it uses the same M5 Pro or M5 Max internally. With rumors that the M6 Pro and M6 Max are being skipped entirely, you’ll have to accept that you’re paying a lot more for the same performance. To make the decision harder, Apple still sells the previous-gen model—so you’ll have to decide whether the upgraded screen is worth the $400 extra. For my money, it totally is.

Meanwhile, Windows has made its first successful attempt to properly compete with the MacBook Pro. I’m talking primarily about the launch of Nvidia’s new RTX Spark “superchip” and the new laptops that use it. To be clear, despite Nvidia’s involvement, these aren’t gaming laptops. Like the MacBook Pro, they’re designed first and foremost for running heavier creative applications and on-device AI. The Surface Laptop Ultra is a great example, which has a lot in common with the standard 15-inch Surface Laptop. But the differences internally are substantial. The Surface Laptop Ultra uses a single chip that integrates the CPU, GPU, and memory together, allowing up to 128 GB of memory to be shared across the system. That’s not unlike how Apple Silicon works, dramatically increasing on-device AI performance. So, if you’ve been curious about running LLMs right on your laptop without relying on the cloud, these RTX Spark laptops are a great place to start. The other two RTX Spark laptops I tested, the HP OmniBook Ultra 16 and Lenovo Pro 9n, share a lot with the Surface Laptop Ultra (including performance). The OmniBook Ultra is the thinnest of the three, but I prefer the Surface Laptop Ultra’s Mini-LED display and 3:2 aspect ratio.

It has been revealed that perhaps the most common use for extra laptop performance, however, is gaming. If you strategy to boot up graphically intensive games more than a couple of times a week, you will want a dedicated gaming laptop. After testing dozens over the past year, I’ve come back to the Lenovo LOQ 15 as my top pick. There are cheaper RTX 5050 models, such as the Alienware 15 or MSI Cyborg A15, but prices have been increasing on these laptops over the past few months. The Alienware 15 with the RTX 5050, in particular, has seen a $600 price jump, which makes it incredibly overpriced.

In a recent development, that’s led me back to the LOQ 15, which has stayed steady at $1,300 at Walmart and gives you an RTX 5060 for graphics and a bright, colorful screen. You won’t find a cheaper gaming laptop that doesn’t make some significant compromises in either performance or screen quality, both of which can sour the gaming experience. And while I wish the LOQ 15 were still selling for under $1,000 as it did at launch, it’s still the best gaming laptop for the money right now. It’s really the only gaming laptop under $1,500 I’d currently buy, given where prices are.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also a whole world of gaming laptops outside the budget tier, though. I’ve tested an assortment of options, and I always come back to the Razer Blade 14 and Razer Blade 16. Portable, minimalist, and extremely well-made, their sleek design works just as well for school or work as it does for gaming, without the bulk of a traditional gaming laptop. While you can buy more powerful options, nothing quite matches the Razer Blade. They’re expensive, but if you can afford them, they’re as premium as gaming laptops get. I’ll soon be testing the latest version of the Blade 16, which includes Intel’s latest Panther Lake chips and should offer vastly improved battery life.

According to recent reports, if you choose one of the laptops above, you will be very happy with your purchase. However, if you are looking for a specific feature or a different price point, I have included a few other options below that I’ve recently reviewed and enjoyed using. Each of these recently tested laptops has at least one minor drawback, but they could still be the perfect choice depending on your needs and current discounts.

It has been revealed that framework Laptop 13 Pro for $1,599: We’ve always loved Framework laptops at WIRED, mainly because their internal components are so repairable and upgradable. Customers can easily swap out nearly every part, including the CPU. The Framework Laptop 13 Pro uses the same internal structure as the basic Framework Laptop 13, but upgraded with a haptic touchpad, an aluminum chassis, and a brighter (and sharper) display. The result is the Framework Laptop I’ve always wanted, especially with an all-black aesthetic that hints at ThinkPad inspiration. But most of all, if you’re going to try and make a laptop last for many years, it makes sense that it would be something more premium. This one actually feels like it’s worth the investment.

Microsoft Surface Laptop 13.8 for $1,000: The Surface Laptop 13.8 (also known as the 7th Edition) was one of my favorite laptops throughout 2024 and 2025, primarily because of its premium build quality, great battery life, and 3:2 aspect ratio screen. And while I still love this laptop, it’s risen dramatically in price and no longer feels like a great value, especially since it’s two years old now. The 2024 model now starts at $1,200, though I’ve occasionally seen it dip under $1,000. The next-generation model with the Snapdragon X2 chips costs $1,700, but I have seen that price come down as low as $1,250 on discount.

According to recent reports, dell 14 Plus for $1,172: There was a time—2025, to be exact—when the Dell 14 Plus was as affordable as $600. It was easily the best deal in the world of Windows laptops, primarily because the Dell 14 Plus has a 2560 x 1600 display and a smooth touchpad—two things laptops at that price typically lack. These days, it’s up to over $1,000, though for a 1 TB configuration, that is still a reasonable price. The XPS 13 is the better overall laptop, but the Dell 14 Plus offers more ports and storage for the price.

Lenovo Yoga Slim 7 Ultra for $2,250: I like this laptop quite a bit. The OLED screen is sharp, bright, and quite colorful—very similar to the HP OmniBook Ultra. It also has many of the other great features on premium Windows laptops these days, including a haptic-feedback touchpad and a very slim profile. Unfortunately, it’s only available right now in a very expensive, maxed-out configuration with 32 GB of RAM and at least a terabyte of storage. I don’t think that’s a good pairing for this ultra-light laptop. Even with half the memory and storage, though, this would be too expensive compared to the competition.

Industry observers note that macBook Pro M5 for $1,999: It’s not a significant step up from the MacBook Air in performance, and it’s much thicker. You’re paying for the Mini-LED screen and extra ports. Unfortunately, compared to the other MacBook models, it got a $300 price bump to $1,999. On discount, you’ll often find it selling for $1,799, though, which is solid for the specs.

In a recent development, asus Zenbook A16 for $2,200: The Zenbook A14 and A16 are Asus’ ultralight laptops, weighing just 2.16 pounds, making them some of the lightest laptops you can buy right now. This second-generation Zenbook A16 is still incredibly light and now comes with second-generation Snapdragon X2 chips. It’s unique for its portability, and the Qualcomm chips deliver great battery life and performance. However, given the dramatic price increase, I’d suggest buying the 2025 model instead, which consistently comes in under $1,000.

Alienware 16X Aurora for $2,575: Another solid gaming laptop with the typical Alienware flair. Its standout features are its higher-resolution display and great build quality. The price fluctuates frequently, though, and in most cases, the LOQ 15 is the better option (unless you really want that sharper OLED screen, which is this laptop’s best quality).

According to recent reports, asus Googlebook 14: While I love the Android integration and the beauty of this hardware, this particular Googlebook is far too expensive for what these devices can actually do. They fill a very familiar role to Chromebooks, and yet, these first Googlebooks all have 16 GB of RAM for some reason. This one just doesn’t earn its $1,200 price tag.

Dell 14S: This is the 2026 successor to the Dell 14 Plus, which I recommended above. This is a solid laptop with a premium design and a highly reflective OLED display. It also performs well, thanks to the latest Intel Core Ultra Series 3 chip. But it’s far too expensive right now. Until the price comes down, I prefer just about every other Dell option, including the Dell 14 Plus, Dell XPS 13, or Dell XPS 14.

Lenovo LOQ 15 Essential: This is a “new” model that came out this year, even though it uses a CPU from 2023. But honestly, this is just too expensive. I’ve seen it on sale for under $1,400, but even then, the standard LOQ 15 costs about the same and has a far superior display.

It has been revealed that acer Swift 16 AI: This is one of the few laptops you can buy with the powerful, efficient fresh Intel Core Ultra X9 chips. However, the Acer Swift 16 AI takes an experimental approach with its oversized trackpad, making it very difficult to use. Even at a discount, you’ll find it frustrating.

Sources indicate that asus TUF Gaming A14: There’s a lot I like about this gaming laptop. The design is portable yet modern, and the display is sharp. And while the TUF Gaming A14 is impressive technically (using the interesting AMD Strix Point chip), the lack of a discrete graphics card doesn’t provide enough gaming performance to justify its very high price. I haven’t tested the options with dedicated graphics cards, but they tend to be more expensive than counterparts from Lenovo, Acer, or Alienware.

Sources indicate that asus Vivobook 14: I recommended this laptop a lot throughout 2025, but it doesn’t hold up as well these days. While the Vivobook 14 has great battery life, the HP OmniBook 5 14 offers a much better display and similar specs, making it a better laptop.

How Much Should You Spend on a Laptop?

It has been revealed that if you’re shopping for a laptop, you probably already have a budget. But some context might help put things in perspective. The cheapest laptops cost around $200, but laptop prices can range as high as $5,000. Meanwhile, the average amount people spend, according to the best data we have, is around $750. That lands decidedly in the midrange, splitting between the more expensive devices that are more than $1,000 and the budget-tier machines you find below $700.

When we talk about pricing, it’s often the “starting” price of the laptop, meaning the lowest-priced configuration. This is really important to consider, as you want to compare devices apples to apples as much as possible. For example, a cheaper laptop might start at $750 with 256 GB of storage, while a more premium laptop might start at this same price but come with 512 GB or even 1 TB of storage. Increasingly, you can find some really decent laptops around this price, some of which we’ve listed.

It has been revealed that if your budget needs to be under $750, though, there are still good options. Laptops below this price tend to come with compromises. Most commonly, it’s the quality of the display and touchpad that suffers, as these are things you can’t gauge from a spec sheet or reference photo. Or it might be a performance-related concern, such as the 8 GB of memory in the MacBook Neo. If you’re shopping for something under $500, Chromebooks often give you the best bang for your buck.

Sources indicate that so, why spend more? Well, there are two primary reasons. First, you might want a more premium design, perhaps one that has a more daring aesthetic or high-end components. Take the MacBook Pro, for example. It starts at $600 more than the MacBook Air but comes with a brighter mini-LED screen, significantly better speakers, and more ports. The second primary reason to spend more than $750 or so is to get more performance. Whether for gaming or content creation, laptops with discrete GPUs cost more, which is why it’s hard to find a worthwhile gaming laptop for less than $1,000. If you’re buying a gaming laptop, plan to spend a few hundred bucks more.

What Are the Best Laptop Brands?

Industry observers note that unlike the smartphone world, the biggest laptop brands have been around for more than 40 years. Besides Apple, four laptop brands stand out for adopting the latest technology and trends while providing reliable support and service.

It has been revealed that lenovo is the biggest PC brand in the world, at least in terms of global shipments. It’s perhaps most well-known for its familiar sub-brands like ThinkPad and Yoga, but it also isn’t afraid to take risks with more experimental designs and advanced technology. Lenovo has also made a name for itself in the gaming space with its Legion laptops, known for balancing performance and features at competitive prices.

Asus has quickly become a favorite, notable for the sheer number of laptops available in the consumer market. The organization takes a similar approach to Lenovo, which has led Asus to innovate quickly on latest technology and designs while also launching premium laptops at more affordable prices than its competitors. Gaming, in particular, is a space Asus has come to dominate, with the ROG Zephyrus, Strix, and TUF brands leading the way.

Dell and HP are generally more conservative, but both have recently undergone significant rebranding. In 2024, HP replaced its Spectre and Envy lines with the OmniBook name. Meanwhile, Dell briefly retired its well-known Inspiron and XPS sub-brands in 2025, though it has since reversed course and brought the XPS line back.

Other notable laptop brands include Microsoft Surface, Samsung, Acer, LG, and MSI, though none have the same global footprint as the top four.

How Do I Choose the Right Laptop?

Industry observers note that if none of these laptops resonate with what you’re looking for, that’s OK! There are far more laptops than we have time to test. To help you make smart choices, we put together a complete laptop buying guide. We also cover the CPUs and GPUs you need to know. We recommend sticking to these guidelines:.

RAM: We recommend 16 GB of RAM. That’s become the newly introduced standard, even in more affordable laptops. Upgrading to 32 GB is even better, so you won’t have to worry about running out of memory, especially if you’re a gamer or video editor. The recent memory shortage has led to some dramatic price increases, largely based on configurations of RAM. Apple’s launch of the 8 GB MacBook Neo this spring has led to the return of high-end 8-GB Windows laptops as well, such as the Dell XPS 13.

CPU: For Windows laptops, you have three CPU brands to choose from: Intel, AMD, or Qualcomm. Intel’s Core Ultra Series 2 launched in late 2024 and delivers a huge boost to battery life. It also has the best integrated graphics of the three. Core Ultra Series 3 is just now rolling out and, based on my testing, is extremely impressive in performance and efficiency. While AMD chips are primarily used in gaming laptops, they’ve struggled to gain ground on Intel elsewhere.

It has been revealed that qualcomm’s Snapdragon X chips, however, have seriously challenged Intel over the past year with their ARM architecture, offering some of the best battery life we’ve ever seen on Windows machines. The second generation, Snapdragon X2, was confirmed last fall and rolled out slowly throughout 2026. They improve performance, but in many cases, they've led to more expensive laptops, while previous-gen laptops are still available that cost less.

In a recent development, starting this year, there’s also the choice of Nvidia’s fresh RTX Spark platform, which gives you the option of 18-core or 20-core CPUs. More on that in the GPU section below.

Apple Silicon is what powers all the modern MacBooks, the latest of which is the M5 chip. Read our in-depth guide on Which MacBook to Buy for more information.

Graphics: Want to play AAA PC games, edit video on your laptop, or run local AI models? You’ll want some powerful graphics on hand. At this point, Nvidia is the primary option. The RTX 5090, launched in 2025, is still the most powerful latest GPU available, but the 5040-series remains a good option.

Sources indicate that integrated graphics have improved significantly over the years, though, especially on processors made by Apple, AMD, and Intel, such as the Apple M5 or the Intel Core Ultra X9 388H. Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform uses a single “superchip” that provides unified memory to both the CPU and GPU to improve AI performance.

Industry observers note that screen: The display depends highly on the size of the laptop. A 1,200-pixel resolution (HD+) screen on a 13- or 14-inch laptop looks sharp enough to get by, but you’ll want more pixels on larger displays, such as a 2560 x 1600, 2880 x 1800, or 3840 x 2400. While IPS screens are good enough for most people, OLED and Mini-LED are becoming more common, offering better color accuracy, deeper contrast, and excellent HDR performance.

Connectivity: We generally recommend at least two USB-C ports, along with one HDMI and one USB-A port for legacy devices. (Remember that nearly all laptops today use one of those USB-C ports for the power adapter.) Thankfully, most laptops still have headphone jacks, but always check, because a few models have dropped them. Lastly, make sure it supports Wi-Fi 6E or newer. Even if you don’t have a Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7 router yet, you’ll likely have one in the future (see our Best Routers or Best Mesh Systems guides if you need a upcoming one).

Battery life: Battery life is extremely competitive these days, with Apple, Qualcomm, and Intel all making highly ambitious battery-life claims. Most laptops with the latest chips (and without discrete graphics) will get you more than 10 hours of battery life, or many more if your workload is lighter.

As mentioned, in Windows-based laptops, there are three primary options for CPUs: Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm. All three companies offer good processors, but it really depends on the type of laptop. For premium laptops, you’ll want something like the Intel Core Ultra 258V or Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite. Meanwhile, for budget laptops, Snapdragon X is the best choice. And for gaming laptops, I’d recommend something from AMD, such as the Ryzen AI 9 365. All three companies have announced next-gen chips for 2026, and there’s some exciting stuff coming soon.

Intel’s latest chips, known as either Core Ultra Series 3 or codename Panther Lake, are slowly rolling out in new laptops, such as the Dell XPS 14. These chips represent a massive leap forward in both CPU and integrated graphics performance. While highly impressive, they will soon face fresh competition from upcoming AMD and Qualcomm releases.

Industry observers note that qualcomm made a major impact in 2024 with its Snapdragon X chips. Similar to Apple’s M-series, these ARM-based processors prioritize efficiency to drastically improve battery life. This has been a game-changer for Windows laptops across different price points. The Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite is the highest-end option for performance, but the Snapdragon X Plus and base Snapdragon X still offer equally strong battery life, despite showing up in much cheaper laptops. The sequel was unveiled in late 2025, and now in 2026, we’re seeing those laptops roll out. Unfortunately, like Intel’s latest chips, laptops with this next-gen silicon tend to be significantly more expensive than their predecessors.

In a recent development, AMD has grown into a competitive player in the gaming laptop space. Its latest processors, including the Ryzen 9 9950X3D and 9900X3D, are the most powerful gaming chips you can find in a laptop. Unfortunately, it’s still hard to find many laptops supporting these killer chips. AMD also offers its Ryzen AI 300 H and HX chips, which are more commonly found in gaming laptops. While they also offer a mainstream Ryzen AI 300 series, these chips aren’t found in many laptops and at the moment fall short of the battery life offered by Intel and Qualcomm.

Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform just hit the scene, promising to deliver power and efficiency, especially when running AI-based operations. It’s not as ubiquitous as Intel, AMD, or Qualcomm chips, but it’s something to watch for.

It has been revealed that I have been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, and WIRED contributor Chris Null has been testing them for 25 years. We test each laptop we review in a variety of situations, including both synthetic benchmark tests and real-world use cases. We make comparisons against similar equipment. We don’t just look at the specs—our reviews evaluate performance, usability, portability, and price to help you find the right laptop for your needs.

We put every laptop through a gauntlet of tests before writing a review and assigning a rating.

Sources indicate that hands-on use: We evaluate the exterior of the device. We compare how thin and light it is against other laptops. We repeatedly open and close the lid to test the quality and ease of the hinge. We push on weak points like the keyboard and lid to test build quality. We also extensively test the keyboard and touchpad for comfort and precision. By using each laptop as our daily driver for days or even weeks, we can spot real-world quirks—like awkward port placement, excessive bloatware, or unexpected problems that may make the laptop difficult to use—that you won’t see on a spec sheet.

Recent findings suggest that sights and sounds: Once we boot up the device, it’s all about the sights and sounds. The screen is paramount, as it’s your window into everything the laptop has to offer. While you can tell a lot about brightness, color, and contrast just by looking, we go beyond subjective testing. We use a Spyder colorimeter to precisely measure brightness, contrast, color saturation, and accuracy. For HDR-capable screens, we also test peak brightness with HDR content. Finally, we evaluate the webcam and speakers to ensure they are ready for your video calls and streaming sessions.

Recent findings suggest that performance testing: Finally, we test performance. We always evaluate a laptop based on what it’s intended for—we don’t expect a $500 budget laptop to run like a gaming powerhouse, or a gaming rig to get 18 hours of battery life. Our testbed includes more than 20 synthetic benchmarks, which we constantly adapt based on the device's CPU and operating system. These include tests within Geekbench, PCMark, 3DMark, Procyon, GFXBench, Puget Bench, Superposition, Cinebench, and various gaming-related tests such as 3DMark and Cyberpunk 2077. While we don’t generally report raw scores, we pay close attention to what they tell us. We also monitor fan noise, surface temperature, and overall battery life during these tests.

It’s a lot, I know. But we’re thorough, because we want to stand by our recommendations and ensure that the laptops we rate highly are worth the money.

Upside Foods can now make a million pounds of chicken a year without killing any animals

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that upside Foods didn’t even have to try to garner interest from MrBeast, the most-followed creator on the internet.
  • It has been revealed that the eleven-year-old firm had undergone a 10,000-fold scale-up that it hopes could revolutionize the nascent cultivated meat industry.
  • So MrBeast, whose real name is Jimmy Donaldson, came to see for himself, taste-testing two chicken sandwiches on camera, one made with meat from a chicken killed that day, and one using Upside Foods chicken.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that upside Foods didn’t even have to try to garner interest from MrBeast, the most-followed creator on the internet. The YouTuber demonstrated up at the company’s facility with his video crew.

It has been revealed that the eleven-year-old firm had undergone a 10,000-fold scale-up that it hopes could revolutionize the nascent cultivated meat industry. Upside states it can now make over one million pounds of edible, cultivated chicken each year without killing a single animal in the process. Such an achievement challenges the long-held industry skepticism over whether lab-grown meat will ever be affordable enough to meaningfully scale.

So MrBeast, whose real name is Jimmy Donaldson, came to see for himself, taste-testing two chicken sandwiches on camera, one made with meat from a chicken killed that day, and one using Upside Foods chicken. He was unable to identify which sandwich was which — they tasted exactly the same to him.

“I mean, you see me in the video – I was like, ‘Oh my gosh, what is he going to say?’” Upside Foods CEO Dr. Uma Valeti told TechCrunch. “I thought he would maybe say a nice thing here and there, but he would get it right. But he didn’t.”.

Recent findings suggest that if there was any reason to doubt Donaldson’s assessment, now you can taste the chicken yourself, if you live in California. Upside Foods unveiled on Tuesday that it will now be available at several restaurants in the state, marking a major milestone for the cultivated meat industry.

Sources indicate that “This has been a decade of foundation building,” Valeti stated, adding that Upside Foods has secured its next set of regulatory approvals from the FDA and USDA. “With that comes the whole excitement and ice-breaking for the field … There’s brilliant ideas in science, but science only makes an impact when you get to scale.”.

Solving this scale problem has been the biggest obstacle for the cultivated meat industry. The first ever lab-grown hamburger, produced in 2013, cost $300,000 to make. Now, Valeti indicates that Upside Foods can match the price range of “really high quality organic chicken.”.

“The whole industry was going through this really difficult scale-up period… We had to go through that grinder to come out on the other side,” Valeti noted.

The cultivated meat movement isn’t just about animal welfare (though for many, that’s a plus). According to the Good Food Institute, a nonprofit think tank for alternative proteins, it would take 5.5 Earths to feed the world with conventional meat production in 2050, when the United Nations predicts that the global population will approach 10 billion.

In a recent development, “We use less water, less land, less energy,” Valeti remarked. “The power of this technology is you protect the choice of eating what we love, but we can also protect everything else we love about protecting life, and the environment, and animal welfare.”.

The process of cultivating meat also cuts the risk of E. coli, Salmonella, and antibiotic resistance while lowering cholesterol and saturated fat, the tech giant promises. Upside Foods’ chicken is also augmented with soy protein isolate, pea fiber, and olive oil, making it more nutritionally dense. Valeti says that this doesn’t affect the flavor, which is something he agonized over. He even brought in Michelin-starred and James Beard Award-winning chefs, Thomas Keller and Nancy Silverton, to weigh in on the taste.

According to recent reports, “We got a lot of confidence after we worked with [these chefs],” Valeti remarked. “They said, ‘Uma, you and your team are obsessing too much about it. The majority of people, when you put this in your chicken dishes, will not be able to tell.’”.

Recent findings suggest that upside Foods’ milestone of producing one million pounds of chicken per year is meaningful, but the industry still has a long way to go. In 2021, it was estimated that Americans consume about 8 billion chickens annually. But aside from sheer capital, Valeti believes the firm has been able to scale the amount it has because of how much it has learned by experimenting with the process over the years. He thinks more growth is possible.

“Unless we show it at the largest scale possible that anybody has done, no one is going to believe us,” he said.

#760. Breaking: Neurable One review: The brain-scanning headphones that helped me stay focused

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2206 w)

Breaking: Neurable One review: The brain-scanning headphones that helped me stay focused

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2206 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The cans hide a wearable EEG that tracks your attention.
  • I've always been fascinated by the inner workings of the human mind, and I've tested plenty of brain gadgets in my time.
  • It has been revealed that the tech giant describes it as a "fitness tracker for your brain," so when your attention starts to drift, the headphones will remind you to keep your focus where it needs to be.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The cans hide a wearable EEG that tracks your attention.

I've always been fascinated by the inner workings of the human mind, and I've tested plenty of brain gadgets in my time. Sadly, all of them have been so clunky that they can only really be worn in the privacy of your own home. At least, that was the case. The Neurable One actually buries its brain-scanning technology into a pair of beefy over-ear headphones. It's designed to keep an eye on your focus levels and attention while you work, or meditate, wherever you are.

It has been revealed that the tech giant describes it as a "fitness tracker for your brain," so when your attention starts to drift, the headphones will remind you to keep your focus where it needs to be. And, if things continue to go wayward, you'll be advised to take a break and come back fresh rather than burning out halfway through the day. In that regard, it's been fascinating to see how the system thinks my brain operates on a regular basis.

Industry observers note that the Neurable One is cheaper than its predecessors and its competitors, and Neurable has improved its software platform. If there's a downside, it's that as much as I've loved my time with them, it's hard to think anyone other than nerds like me will want to use them.

Industry observers note that neurable spun out of a project from the University of Michigan in 2015, with the goal of building Brain Computer Interfaces (BCIs) and algorithms to interpret that data. The focus is on cognitive performance as there's plenty of military and civilian applications for the technology. Despite the name, Neurable One is actually the third pair of EEG headphones the organization has made. In 2024, it partnered with Master & Dynamic on the MW75 Neuro, and a year later the Neuro LT, a lighter version of the same product addressing user comfort complications. This time out, Neurable is going it alone without the backing of any fancy audio brands.

Recent findings suggest that at a glance, you'll struggle to notice much difference between this and its predecessors, as any variances are mostly aesthetic tweaks. Button placements are the same, but they're now pill-shaped rather than the circles found on the older models. The logo on the earcups has changed from M&D's icon to Neurable's signature brainwave, and there are fewer vents. In fact, the biggest difference is the loss of the cantilevered armatures joining the headband to the earcups, which have been replaced with standard hardware here.

In a recent development, it's a similar story inside the body as well; the Neurable One is more or less equipped with the same gear as before. You'll get the same 40mm Beryllium drivers, Bluetooth 5.2, AAC and aptX, albeit with six microphones — down from the eight on the MW75 Neuro. As before, each earcup has a series of dry-fit EEG sensors woven into the earpads which sit around your ear.

Sources indicate that neurable's pitch is to help people gain deeper insights into their own cognitive performance through the day. It contends that, much like the rest of our body, our minds have enough fuel to get us through the day, but not at full-tilt, full-pelt output. The company indicates it's a better idea to, when your attention and focus starts to wane, take a break ahead of you burning out. Neurable argues that spending a quick five minutes staring out of the window is better than getting a headache and not functioning for an hour.

Strap the headphones on at the start of the day and the system will keep an eye on how you're doing. Do this over a period of days, or weeks, and you'll get a sense of where your focus is at its highest and lowest. You can then adjust your working patterns to suit those stats. The Neurable One works equally well when you're meditating or relaxing, giving you insights as to how and when your mind rests.

According to recent reports, one of my eternal gripes with a lot of wearable EEGs (and other fabric sensors more broadly) is that the sensor pads are often fussy. They often don't work at all if they're bone dry and the skin they're in contact with is dry as well, which frustrates me. I've regularly had to gently dab the pads with cold water before running a washcloth across my forehead to dampen it. But, if the skin and pads are too wet, you'll be given a warning to dry both out, which slows you down even further. Thankfully, the Neurable One's dry-fit sensors worked from the get-go more or less every time I've used them. Every now and again, I'll be asked to push my (short) hair away from around my ears to improve the connection, but it's a world away from other products in the same field that I've tested.

According to recent reports, setup is a breeze, and the process of beginning your first session is relatively effortless, as is the daily routine you're expected to fall into. That begins with a check in at the start of the day, closing your eyes and triggering a 60-second scan of your brain. You'll get a dashboard containing your scores, with a comparison to the day before to see if things got better or worse. If you had a rough night, or if there's a lot going on, you can journal some notes on the same pane.

Industry observers note that what's far more interesting and useful are the Insights and Improve sections, which tell you both what to do to manage your cognitive load right now, and how to boost it. The former suggests that you delay big decisions, not starting jobs that need a lot of attention and grouping small, repetitive tasks together. The latter asks you to go for a quick walk in the sun, go sit in another room away from your computer for five minutes or to write down all of the things sitting in your mental cache. Once done, you can run another check-in to see if that's made any improvement.

If I'm honest, I was having a busy day at the start of a busy week, and felt snowed under by all of the projects on my desk. (In fact, my biggest concern, throughout testing these headphones, was that my Cognitive Load was always problematically high. It's almost as if working in journalism and juggling hundreds of projects all at once is somehow a problem.) The app told me that I was running low, but remarked I should walk up and down my stairs for a few minutes and then come back and check again. And, wouldn't you know, it actually did improve both my score and my ability to get stuff done for the rest of the morning.

Industry observers note that most days, I would set the EEG running at 9AM or so and not take them off until 12 or 1PM. The app will keep track of how well it thinks you're concentrating, letting you see that as a real time figure on screen. If it detects your focus beginning to drift, it'll rouse you back, but after a while, if you still struggle to concentrate, it'll advise you to take a short break. One thing I don't like is the way the system prods you to get back on track: When it thinks your focus is waning, you'll get a ping played in your ear as a sort of "come on, pay attention" trigger.

In a recent development, it's a harsh noise, and one that would distract me as often as it did help me drift back toward focus. You can shut off this guidance in the app, but I persevered with them even when it put me in mind of a '70s kung fu B-movie where the protagonist is asked to build a house of cards while being pelted with rotten fruit. Regularly, I'd be halfway through writing a line in what I'd describe as a flow state and then I'd get pinged, knocking me off my train of thought.

Recent findings suggest that but the more I used the headphones, the more I was able to see when the system noted I was doing well and what caused slips. It became an increasingly positive feedback loop where I'd scrub through the timeline of my morning to see what I was doing when my focus was high.

As for audio quality, it's clear the tech giant has tried to sail close to Master & Dynamic's promise of warm bass and clear treble. There's a wonderful atmosphere to the sound that makes you feel like you're in the room when it was recorded. One of my favourite tracks to test headphones with is "Finale" from the Tron: Legacy soundtrack where you can hear the horn player's breath. Wearing these, I was equally delighted to feel the rumble of the kettle drums pushing the air to my ear as they crescendoed.

Industry observers note that the downside of Neurable no longer working with an established audio brand is that the One loses the added-value features inside the app. Whereas the previous models had a custom EQ you could fiddle with to your heart's content, here you just get the default tuning. That's not a bad thing as the audio quality here is certainly good enough, but I hope this feature can be added later. The other problem is that the app doesn't really have any sort of integration with your music app of choice, and instead will just play generic synthwave by default. Thankfully it will keep running in the background while you switch to Spotify to play actual music as you go.

Interestingly, the original MW75 Neuro weighed in at 338 grams, which was heavy enough to force the company into making a lighter version. The Neuro LT was stated to be 12 percent lighter, and you would have hoped that the Neurable One would continue that trend. Instead, it's rated for 345 grams, making it slightly heavier than the original. (In fact, the only pair of substantial-name cans that beats it for weight are the AirPods Max 2, which weigh in at 386.2 grams.) After a few hours of wearing the Neurable One on my head each day, I really became aware of their presence. I'll admit, I'm not an over-ears person, and so maybe those who are don't mind the sensation of having their ears pinned back for most of the day.

Recent findings suggest that as for battery life, Neurable states the One will run for 22 hours, or 12 hours if you're using the EEG. When using the EEG, without ANC, I got just over 12 hours of use from the headphones before needing to head to the charger. On one hand, that's more than enough time on a charge, on the other, I'd be negligent if I didn't point out it's far below the standard for premium headphones.

At $499, Neurable One is a lot cheaper than the previous versions, and you get all of the insights and data on offer, without any additional paywall. There aren't many companies making consumer-grade EEG headphones, and so Neurable doesn't have much competition. The only real alternative is Brainbit which makes EEG cans for researchers, but I've asked, and it mentioned it does sell its headphones to consumers as well. They will set you back $900, and come with a free iOS, macOS, Android or Windows app to help you monitor your mind.

Naturally, if you're looking for a wearable EEG that isn't built into headphones, then you also have the option of Muse. Its latest is the Muse S Athena, an EEG headband designed to help improve your meditation, but it can also monitor your brain's oxygenation levels. It'll set you back $539 with a year of Muse's premium, which adds in data about your Alpha Peak and Brain Recharge, plus it integrates with Spotify, Calm or your audiobook player of choice.

If you'd rather just buy a pair of high-end headphones, you should instead head to Engadget's guide to the best on the market. It should go without saying that you can pick up plenty of better headphones for less — including Sony's class-leading XM6s.

According to recent reports, I've spent a lot of time second-guessing my own recommendation, because on its own merits this is a great product. It does what it promises in an easy to use, accessible way and it's far cheaper than its (handful of) competitors. In that vacuum, it's well worth the cash, and I think I've meaningfully benefited from my time with this device. If you can afford it, and you're truly keen on learning more about how your own brain works, then I think it's worth it.

The caveat here is that it really does need to be people who are committed to doing this work on a regular basis. I suspect we're a generation or two away from a version of these cans which are truly usable by the mainstream more broadly.

The arrival of the new flagship Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max might be dominating the headlines, but the Chinese smartphone giant also just lifted the curtain on a range of accessories that are worth paying attention to.

If you're a fan of open-ear audio, then the new Xiaomi Clip earbuds are going to be the start of the new reveals. They're the brand's first clip-on model, and weigh just 5.5g per earbud.

It has been revealed that if you're not familiar with this relatively recent trend, clip-on earbuds attach to your ears with a gentle clamping mechanism rather than being pushed inside your ear canal like conventional buds. This makes them highly comfortable and leaves your ear canals open to allow in background noise like traffic or conversations.

They're not a good fit for a loud commute, but such designs have become a popular choice for fitness or scenarios where you want to maintain full situational awareness while still being able to enjoy some tunes.

Xiaomi promises that the Clip earbuds will feel like they're "barely there" while in use, and accommodate a wide range of ear shapes thanks to their flexible shape-memory alloy bridge material.

Industry observers note that fashion is clearly a focus, and the Xiaomi Clip earbuds are offered in four distinct colorways: Sand Gold, Pearl White, Graphite Black, and Frost Purple. They all come with a compact charging case that's designed to look something like a jewelry box.

Sources indicate that as for the more technical specs, each bud contains an 11mm dynamic driver. They offer Hi-Res certified sound and support the modern LHDC 5.0 codec. According to Xiaomi, the battery life comes in at 9 hours of music playback, with an additional 29 hours offered by the charging case.

They cost £129.99 and are available via the Mi website.

There's no better companion for a new Android smartphone than a compatible smartwatch, and Xiaomi has you covered there too with the new Watch S5 41mm.

This £199.99 smartwatch boasts a 1.32 AMOLED display with up to 3,000 nits of peak brightness. It runs Xiaomi HyperOS 4 and is the first Xiaomi Watch S model compatible with Google Wallet – so you can conveniently pay with your wrist without the need for Xiaomi Pay.

Sources indicate that it comes packed with a range of sensors, including a heart rate sensor with blood oxygen sensing capabilities, an accelerometer, gyroscope, ambient light sensor, and temperature sensor. Xiaomi also says that the watch can last up to 14 days on a single charge.

According to recent reports, it's available in three color options: Black, Light Blue, and Ceramic White. Black and Light Blue both offer stainless steel bezels and rubber straps, while Ceramic White has a ceramic bezel and comes with a leather strap.

Finally, Xiaomi is refreshing its affordable smart band. The Xiaomi Smart Band 11 starts at just £54.99 and offers a bright 1.72-inch AMOLED display and the ability to read notifications and see call alerts, in addition to tracking your fitness.

There is a wide range of color options available, with different build materials depending on what you pick. The standard Midnight Black, Glacier Silver, Mystic Rose, and Moon Gold models feature an aluminum frame.

If you want a band with NFC capabilities, you can also pick up the crisp white ceramic edition or a full-metal unibody model in lavender.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Key Apple memory supplier SK Hynix has warned that RAM and flash memory shortages are likely to last through at least 2030, keeping product prices high.
  • Patch: Apple is reportedly about to sign a similar contract with Samsung, also permitting market-driven price increases.
  • SK Hynix says that while AI continues to drive demand and growth, there is little that can be done in the short to medium term to increase supply.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Key Apple memory supplier SK Hynix has warned that RAM and flash memory shortages are likely to last through at least 2030, keeping product prices high. Apple is believed to be one of 14 customers who have locked in priority orders, but the contract does not protect against price increases related to the balance of supply and demand.

Patch: Apple is reportedly about to sign a similar contract with Samsung, also permitting market-driven price increases.

SK Hynix says that while AI continues to drive demand and growth, there is little that can be done in the short to medium term to increase supply.

Supply, on the other hand, is not keeping pace with the growth of the market. Given technical difficulty of leading-edge processes and the long lead time required to build newly introduced production facilities, it expects the structure in which demand exceeds supply to persist through 2030.

The Register reports that SK Hynix has long-term deals with 14 tech giants for priority orders, but these allow for market-based price increases.

Recent findings suggest that 14 big buyers […] will collectively buy more than half of its output during 2027 and 2028, and some of them want to extend those agreements. The Korean giant doesn’t mind that because the deals include “a mechanism that reflects market conditions within a price range agreed upon with customers”.

Apple is used to being in the driving seat when it comes to negotiating with suppliers, but this is not the case where memory and flash storage is concerned. Here, the shortages mean that it will have been forced to agree to contracts that allow significant price hikes in order to obtain guaranteed supplies.

In a recent development, nikkei Asia also reports that printed circuit boards may be the next component to experience constrained supply. Once a humble commodity item, advances in the technology has turned them into specialist tech, with more layers and higher bandwidth requirements. The report says “that complexity shrinks the supplier pool and extends lead times.”.

Apple stated back in June that the organization was doing its best to mitigate the price increases, but it has so far been unable to do so.

Shures fresh spatial audio mic was made with creators in mind

💡 Key Takeaways

  • "We know that more and more people — more and more creators — are kind of multidisciplinary, especially for folks who are maybe video first and then they have to worry about audio second," Steve Marek, Associate Product Manager at Shure, mentioned in a briefing with Mashable.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, spatial audio is having a moment in the creator-verse. Just last month, Sony introduced its ECM-AX10 spatial audio mic, and now Shure is entering the category with its USB-C MV360 and MV360+ spatial audio microphones.

"We know that more and more people — more and more creators — are kind of multidisciplinary, especially for folks who are maybe video first and then they have to worry about audio second," Steve Marek, Associate Product Manager at Shure, mentioned in a briefing with Mashable. "So, we know that there's room for that industry to grow.".

Marek stated, "We really wanted to think of this as a microphone that people can grow with," and that rather than having five different audio recording tools, creators can do everything with the MV360 and have flexibility with their audio output.

According to recent reports, the MV360 retails for $349 and is available now. The microphone kit comes with the USB-C mic, a tripod, a cold shoe mic clip, a 5/8-inch mic clip, a phone clamp, two USB-C cables, a carrying case, and a foam windscreen. The microphone also has an onboard 3.5mm headphone jack.

The MV360 features four capture modes: mono, stereo, immersive binaural, and auto tracking. The latter uses virtual microphones that steer toward the loudest sound source and is ideal for recording podcasts, interviews, or moving subjects. Regardless of capture mode, you'll get a ready-to-use two-channel audio file that requires no post-production work — though it is compatible with editing apps and devices should you want to adjust or edit.

The MV360 can be as simple or as complex as you want. If you're a skilled audio engineer, you can mix to your heart's desire. Or if you've never seen audio software in your life, you have perfectly good sound straight from the mic.

The MV360+ is not available yet, but will be the more advanced option geared toward field recordists, videographers, and VR storytellers. It'll pair with DSLR cameras, action cameras, and 360 cameras. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Recent findings suggest that shure's MOTIV app is where you can set your capture mode and edit audio that you've recorded. There are plenty of presets and adjustable settings that you can play around with, too. Slide the level adjuster to capture every minor sound for ASMR or to avoid audio spiking. You can even select where the microphone is oriented in relation to the subject — whether it's facing up, down, or on its side. There's a little diagram in the app that shows a sound heat map, so you can see exactly from which direction sound is hitting the microphone.

According to recent reports, you can record and edit directly in the app. And one really cool feature is that you can move "virtual microphones" after you've already recorded to better boost directional sound.

I received a test unit of the MV360 microphone ahead of its launch and have had a chance to play around with it a bit. It sounds great for unboxing videos — it picks up on all the crispy sounds without sounding blown out. I tested some whispering ASMR, and I was able to boost the audio levels in the companion app before recording to really pick up on every minor sound. I will be using this as an excuse to buy a bunch of weird candy from Five Below to further test the microphone's ASMR-ability, so stay tuned for that. We'll have a full review of the MV360 coming later.

My only minor frustration with the microphone is how bulky/heavy it is. With pocket mics, like the DJI Mic Mini, there's a small receiver that you plug into your phone. The MV360 plugs directly into your phone or computer via USB-C, so it's tethered to your recording device. Clamping my phone and the mic to the tripod was just a little clunky when oriented in portrait mode. But its heft also makes sense, considering how much more advanced the audio recording is compared to small creator mics.

Also, I love that Shure includes a tripod with the MV360, but I found myself reaching for my personal tripod for most of my recordings.

Neither of those are reason enough to discredit the microphone at all — just some minor learning curves.

The MV360 is available now from Shure and third-party retailers like Amazon for $349. The MV360+ will be available in early 2027 for $449.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was one of three root causes for the outage that affected business, hospitals, governments and other organizations worldwide.

In a recent development, microsoft has revealed more details about the outage that took services like Outlook, Teams and Copilot 365 offline, affecting businesses, hospitals, law enforcement and other organizations around the world. Charles Lamanna, the organization's EVP for Copilot and AI Agents, explained on X that there were three root causes for the outage.

He stated that Microsoft typically maintains two network gateway systems that connect separate systems and allow data to pass between them. One of those gateways wasn't working for Microsoft Teams, and it overwhelmed the primary gateway. It also just so happened that nearly 14 percent of the capacity for that gateway was out of service due to an unrelated concern that happened the previous day. Those two factors caused that gateway to encounter a latent bug that's been in Microsoft's systems since July.

Recent findings suggest that together, the higher load that overwhelmed the gateway, the reduced server capacity and the latent bug led to a build up in traffic requests until Microsoft's servers gave out and stopped functioning. This all happened on a Thursday afternoon, during peak hours of use in the US.

According to recent reports, the outage lasted for almost a full day. Microsoft worked on fixing the issue overnight, but the bug was months-old at that point, and the firm was unable to simply do a rollback in order to promptly undo the changes it had caused. In addition, its servers were overwhelmed by waiting traffic after returning to service and became unresponsive again.

"We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations," Lamanna wrote on his post. These details are from Microsoft's preliminary post-incident report, and the company stated it will release more details in the final report to be released later this week.

According to recent reports, for years, Google has offered its TPUs, or Tensor Processing Units, as a solution for AI training and inference, but they’ve been largely locked to its Google Cloud infrastructure. Google’s latest generation of TPUs is specialized; here’s how the organization describes the lineup in its recent announcement post:.

Customers don’t need to abandon Nvidia outright for Google to increase its TPU market share, or for Nvidia to face more pressure on price.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Genesis AI has “cracked dexterous manipulation,” CEO and co-founder Zhou Xian says.

To make his case, Xian hosted TechCrunch at Genesis AI’s Silicon Valley facility, where its physical AI model operated a pair of off-the-shelf robotic arms. In one demo, the arms picked up two small cardboard boxes, scanned them, placed them in a larger cardboard box, folded it closed, taped it shut, and then plucked a label off a strip of printer tape and applied it to the box.

Industry observers note that it’s an impressive demo, exactly the kind of complex workflow that today’s robots struggle to complete. And while Genesis wouldn’t let your reporter mess with the robot’s mise en place to test its wiles, the manufacturer did agree to re-run the presentation. During the second go-round, the robot fumbled a box and had a heck of a time peeling the tiny adhesive label off the printer tape. A mistake, but also the kind of edge case that can be used to improve a model—”hiccup data,” a Genesis executive suggests.

This is the exact gap—between a lab demo and reliable automation—that Genesis, and the rest of the humanoid physical AI ecosystem, need to bridge if they want to avoid another robot winter. To do so, Xian’s company is announcing a $500 million Series A round led by Khosla Ventures, Premji Invest, and Eclipse.

Industry observers note that xian and Genesis president Théophile Gervet, who met as graduate students in a Carnegie Mellon University lab, cofounded the tech giant in 2024. Genesis announced its $105 million seed round in July 2025. The company’s strategy is vertical integration: generating the bulk of its own training data, developing its own generative AI model, and doing both in concert with the design and construction of a humanoid robot.

“We wanted to ship the best robot, end-to-end product,” Xian remarked.

The startup’s focus on dexterity — the robot’s ability to do stuff with its hands — and gathering the right data to achieve it sets it apart from competitors like Figure or Agility. Genesis gathers force data (apparently the unlock for effective manipulation) using a sensor-enabled glove. The gloves, and accompanying headset cameras, are worn by more than 100 real workers around the world, whose activities contribute to a training dataset that feeds into the company’s model.

The company’s robots wear the same sensor-equipped gloves, and their “hands” are designed to mimic the proportions of human hands. That fidelity, Xian states, enables the robots’ capabilities in sorting and wire manipulation.

The other big investment the company has made is in simulation. One of its advisers, Minchen Li, is a co-author of an influential physics algorithm used by the startup to create millions of high-fidelity models of the robot’s experience.

Still, about that robot: Xian noted that the manufacturer’s model was more capable when operating Eno, the company’s flagship humanoid robot. But Eno wasn’t ready to demonstrate its abilities for TechCrunch.

Recent findings suggest that A handsome machine bearing more than a hint of the late Steve Jobs’ influence on tech gadgets and their marketing, Eno reflects “the feeling” the company wants to deliver to its customers. That means less of a Terminator-styled metal skeleton and more of an iMac on wheels.

Genesis said it has built 30 to 40 Enos, but wasn’t ready to share how many it would make in the year ahead. The manufacturer would only say that a mass-manufacturing contractor had been chosen to start work next year in the U.S. and that the design of the mass-produced version had been finalized. The company is piloting the machine with a handful of undisclosed customers.

To realize the tech giant’s vision, Xian indicates the key bottleneck is hardware capability, both in mechanical design and in the supply chains needed to produce industrial-grade machines. Right now, the company’s dexterous hands can only operate for a few weeks of regular work before they need to be replaced.

Industry observers note that for truly generalized robotic intelligence, Genesis needs more data. Xian pooh-poohs the finer distinctions between architectures like Vision-Language-Action models and World-Action models. In his view, the software is ultimately transformers and attention, so “what really matters is is the whole infra — the training infrastructure, the data infrastructure, and the quality of the data.” He estimates that “the model architecture contributes to maybe 10% of of the final [result].”.

“I don’t think we expect or we need another fundamental scientific leap,” he told TechCrunch. “No, we have all the recipes. It’s just about execution.”.

Latest Update: Windows 11 actually runs better on 8GB of RAM now

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (999 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.
  • I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.
  • According to recent reports, as recently as the beginning of the year, 16GB of RAM was common on sub-$800 Windows laptops, which helped compensate for an increasingly bloated-feeling Windows 11.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.

I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.

According to recent reports, as recently as the beginning of the year, 16GB of RAM was common on sub-$800 Windows laptops, which helped compensate for an increasingly bloated-feeling Windows 11. But with the cost of RAM skyrocketing this year, 8GB is once again typical for a starting configuration. The MacBook Neo got away with it, but Windows laptops, including Microsoft’s own 13-inch Surface Laptop, could struggle. Microsoft was talking a big game about making Windows faster and more reliable before the RAM crisis really hit, and it now seems like that effort is beginning to bear fruit.

Earlier this month, Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft’s EVP of Windows and devices, detailed in a blog post the improvements the company has made to Windows 11 to address the constraints of 8GB PCs. In it, Davuluri claims, “Windows is now up to 20% more responsive, and multitasking is up to 40% faster in our lab test.”.

In a recent development, the most significant change is in memory management. When there isn’t enough available memory to handle all active data, some of it has to be offloaded (or “paged out”) to storage. And SSDs, especially in lower-cost laptops, are much slower than RAM.

When Windows needs to access data that’s been paged out from the RAM to the SSD, it’s called a hard fault (or page fault). If it happens a lot — say, on a laptop with only 8GB of RAM — it leads to little slowdowns like browser tabs requiring a refresh before you can access them again. Davuluri notes, “Windows can now keep up to 2 GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage, so an app or tab you left open is less likely to reload when you return.”.

To test this, I fired up the same 13-inch Surface Laptop with 8GB of RAM that I reviewed back in July, when I proclaimed eight is not enough for Windows. This laptop was one of the worst examples of RAMageddon’s current stranglehold on computing: With half the RAM of last year’s base model, it struggled to keep up with my regular workload. And this is Microsoft’s hardware.

Microsoft’s own laptop could struggle.

Before updating the Surface to the latest Windows 11 build, I got reacquainted with this laptop and the version of Windows I left it on (25H2, build 26200.8875). It was rough. Running about 20 tabs (on the latest Chrome build) while streaming a 4K YouTube video and using Slack and Signal made everything from clicking tabs to swiping around Windows with trackpad gestures feel sluggish. Chrome tabs and apps would refresh after leaving them in the background for just a short moment. When you’re multitasking and bouncing between many tabs, like when researching something, those refreshes get incredibly frustrating. And the fan was running audibly the whole time. Keeping the Resource Monitor open showed memory hard faults ranging from just under 700 faults per second to 29,000 faults per second, during which Windows ground to a halt. Seeing this number literally go off its chart showed just how badly Windows 11 struggled with memory management on 8GB before the upgrade.

Now, after updating the Surface Laptop to Windows 11 version 26H2, build 26300.9974 (memory improvements are live on build 26300.9818 and beyond) things are much improved. I opened over 30 Chrome tabs while streaming the same 4K YouTube video and running the same chat apps, and Windows slowed a bit, but nowhere near as much. I could feel things like Task View get a little less responsive and at times stuttery, but it was the way you’d expect when taxing a system. Chrome tabs required less frequent refreshes. The fan also took longer to kick in and ran a little quieter and for shorter durations when it did.

Sources indicate that taking a fresh look at the Resource Monitor, hard faults at normal operation were now under 300 per second, with occasional jumps to about 1,000. Performance was even slightly better when I subbed out Chrome for Microsoft Edge. Edge felt more responsive under load and had fewer hard faults when running 30 tabs, the same 4K YouTube video, and a Google Meet video call.

I’m happy to see that the 8GB Surface Laptop now performs better, and I’m equally relieved that Windows 11 is starting to feel more viable on 8GB of RAM. (It’s still a shame the 8GB Surface Laptop costs more than last year’s 16GB, but I digress.) Do I want 8GB of RAM in any laptop I’m personally buying? No.

Sources indicate that as I mentioned when I reviewed the latest Dell XPS 13, I appreciate that 8GB is workable — and it should be fine for basic needs today — but I still advise getting 16GB if you’re able. The extra headroom will keep things speedy for longer, especially after you bog a computer down with lots of files, apps, or games. And as much better as the 8GB Surface Laptop is now, I still managed to crash Chrome entirely with fewer than three dozen tabs. Microsoft has done better by its entry-level laptop, but it’s not a miracle worker.

Our ongoing RAMageddon makes living with lower quantities of memory a grim reality. Microsoft is partly to blame for that, of course. And it hasn’t done itself any favors with all the feature bloat it put into Windows 11 during the Copilot / AI era. Meanwhile, other OSes, like Linux, macOS, and ChromeOS, can get by better with less. Still, I’m glad to see Microsoft ever so slightly right the ship in this one way.

Through the SIM Manager app on Android, the folks over at Android Authority noticed strings that tell a pretty clear story.

A new feature called “Android Fast Switch” would let you “use your phone number on up to two phones,” with the SIM automatically switching to “whichever phone you unlock.”.

“Android Fast Switch” sounds nearly identical to Handoff on iPhone, a feature that lets iPhone owners share one SIM between two iPhones and quickly switch devices on the fly.

We also don’t know what devices may be supported – this could easily end up as a Pixel-only affair.

According to recent reports, as per usual with these early teardowns, though, the actual launch of a feature like this could be weeks, months, or even years away. Still, the idea itself is rather exciting.

Sources indicate that iPhone’s Handoff feature always sounded useful, but I personally always questioned why it would be useful on iPhone. With so little variety in hardware, the utility of switching between two iPhones seems somewhat dubious, outside of perhaps using a Mini or Air as a situational device alongside a Pro device.

Sources indicate that on Android, the combinations are endless. It all just depends on what devices Google supports. What devices would you switch between?
